clue.text: "I it thus" (Johnson)

parts.note: Samuel Johnson's famous retort to Berkeley's idealism, kicking a stone, with its verb left out for the solver to fill in

explanation.walkthrough: The gap in the quotation is the answer: Johnson kicked a large stone and declared he had disproved Bishop Berkeley's claim that matter does not exist.
explanation.definitionFit: To disprove an argument is to rebut it, which is what Johnson claimed his kick did to Berkeley.

clue.text: Venetian fop in outlandish rodeo rig

indicators.note: outlandish means bizarre or strange, so the letters of the following words are put into a strange new order

explanation.surface: A dandy from Venice turns up at a rodeo in bizarre gear.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffle the eight letters of RODEO RIG. The clue as scanned says 'top', a one-letter misread of 'fop', which is what fits the character.
explanation.definitionFit: In Othello this character is a foolish, vain Venetian gentleman gulled by Iago, a classic stage dandy.

clue.text: How K. Winsor's heroine went on and on …

definitions.meaning: Kathleen Winsor's 1944 bestseller is titled ... Amber, after its heroine Amber

explanation.surface: A reader complains that a romance novel's heroine went on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: Winsor's heroine is Amber of the title Forever Amber, and going on and on means lasting for all time.

clue.text: Shakespearean doll

parts.note: reads like a toy or puppet from Shakespeare's time, but Doll is the first name of a tavern woman in Henry IV Part 2

explanation.definitionFit: Doll Tearsheet is the prostitute befriended by Falstaff in Henry IV Part 2, so her surname completes the name.

clue.text: Exaggerated part for a mistress in Measure for Measure

definitions.text: part for a mistress in Measure for Measure
definitions.meaning: Mistress ... is the bawd who keeps a brothel in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure

explanation.surface: A theatre critic calls an actress's performance as a mistress in Measure for Measure exaggerated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exaggerated is overplayed, and Shakespeare named his brothel-keeper Mistress Overdone in Measure for Measure.

clue.text: Avon sand-dune is arranged by its Swan

indicators.note: arranged means set in a new order, so the letters of the preceding words are put in a fresh sequence

explanation.surface: A sand dune on the river Avon is landscaped by the river's own swan.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare was called the Swan of Avon by Ben Jonson, so 'its Swan' is the Avon's poet; rearrange AVON SAND-DUNE IS for the title of his narrative poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare, the Swan of Avon, wrote this narrative poem about the goddess and the hunter in 1593.

clue.text: His writing produced hard cash

parts.note: reads as an author earning good money, but Hard Cash is the title of an 1863 novel by the Victorian writer

explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade, the Victorian novelist, wrote Hard Cash, an exposé of private lunatic asylums.

clue.text: Paper business bound to fold

parts.note: reads like a newspaper or stationery firm certain to go bust, but describes the Japanese craft where paper must be creased

explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of folding paper into models requires every sheet to be creased into shape.

clue.text: Singer's property

definitions.meaning: A novel by the Yiddish writer Isaac Bashevis Singer, sequel to The Manor
land and buildings owned by someone

explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Bashevis Singer wrote the novel The Estate, and a large holding of land is a landed property.

clue.text: Baldwin saw America as one

parts.note: James Baldwin's 1962 novel about race and sexuality in New York takes its title from this phrase, suggesting he felt a stranger at home

explanation.definitionFit: James Baldwin titled his 1962 novel of New York life with this phrase, depicting America as a foreign land to its outsiders.

clue.text: Gascon who saw Maastricht and died

definitions.text: Gascon who saw Maastricht and died

parts.words: Gascon who saw Maastricht and died
parts.note: the real musketeer from Gascony was killed at the siege of Maastricht in 1673, as Dumas also tells

explanation.definitionFit: Dumas' musketeer hero, from Gascony, was based on a real captain killed besieging the Dutch city in 1673.

clue.text: Break a lance, / And run — at death" (Henry VI, Part )

definitions.text: Break a lance, / And run — at death" (Henry VI, Part )

parts.words: Break a lance, / And run — at death" (Henry VI, Part )
parts.note: a line from Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 1 with one word left out for the solver to supply

explanation.walkthrough: The full line is 'And run a-tilt at death', meaning charge at death like a knight with a lance levelled.
explanation.definitionFit: To run tilting is to charge with a lance levelled, as jousting knights did at each other.

clue.text: Describes Ryder's wartime arrival at a castle

definitions.text: Describes Ryder's wartime arrival at a castle

parts.words: Describes Ryder's wartime arrival at a castle
parts.note: Charles Ryder in Waugh's Brideshead ... returns as an army officer to the great house he knew before the war

explanation.definitionFit: Waugh's title says Ryder came back to Brideshead, the grand house, when billeted there in wartime: going there again.

clue.text: He recorded the end of Appleby as Michael! Innes

definitions.text: He recorded the end of Appleby as Michael! Innes

parts.words: He recorded the end of Appleby as Michael! Innes
parts.note: the Oxford don J. I. M. ... wrote detective stories under the pen name Michael Innes, one titled Appleby's End

explanation.definitionFit: The scholar J. I. M. Stewart wrote the Inspector Appleby mysteries, including Appleby's End, under the pseudonym Michael Innes.

clue.text: Shrub found in territory Rob Roy MacGregor seized

indicators.note: found in says the shrub's letters lie within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A bush grows on land that the Scottish outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor took over.
explanation.walkthrough: Rob Roy MacGregor was a Scottish outlaw; the letters run across the end of MacGregor and the start of seized.
explanation.definitionFit: This spiny yellow-flowered bush, also called furze or whin, covers Scottish moorland.

clue.text: Nobel physicist (a good man among German ones)

indicators.note: among says one piece sits in the middle of the other

parts.note: ein is German for one, so two of them give two copies
ST is the abbreviation for saint, a good man

explanation.surface: A Nobel prize physicist was a fine fellow among his German compatriots.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis reads like a biographical aside about a decent man among his countrymen; 'German ones' is the plural of the German numeral, so two copies are needed with the saint between.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein won the 1921 Nobel Prize in physics for explaining the photoelectric effect.

clue.text: Let old -yield the prize" (Dryden)

parts.note: a line from Dryden's Alexander's Feast with the name of a musician left out for the solver to supply

explanation.walkthrough: Dryden's ode closes: 'Let old Timotheus yield the prize, / Or both divide the crown', comparing Alexander's court musician with Saint Cecilia.
explanation.definitionFit: The flute-player in Dryden's ode, court musician to Alexander the Great, is told to yield to Saint Cecilia.

clue.text: Expeditions scared us badly

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of the words before it are put in poor order

explanation.definitionFit: Medieval military campaigns to the Holy Land are the classic example of religious expeditions.

clue.text: Mrs Yeobright (a lifelong Damon fan)

parts.note: in Hardy's Return of the Native the heroine marries Clym Yeobright yet stays drawn to her old lover Damon Wildeve

explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's heroine Eustacia Vye weds Clym Yeobright but still loves Damon Wildeve until both drown.

clue.text: Winter may have been so, yet not unkind, Bridges thought

definitions.text: Winter may have been so, yet not unkind, Bridges thought

parts.words: Winter may have been so, yet not unkind, Bridges thought
parts.note: alludes to a description of winter by the poet Robert Bridges as rough and ungainly but not harsh

explanation.definitionFit: The poet pictured winter as rough-mannered and crude, yet gentle at heart.

clue.text: Mother starts many a toddler's early reading

indicators.note: starts points to the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A mother begins many a small child's first reading lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: Mater is Latin for mother, often used in older British slang for one's mum.
explanation.definitionFit: Mater is Latin for mother, used jokingly in public-school English for one's mum.

clue.text: Whirlwind creation by Conrad

definitions.meaning: Joseph Conrad's 1902 novella about a steamship caught in a great storm

explanation.surface: A whirlwind piece of writing by Joseph Conrad.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical cyclone of the western Pacific, and the title of Conrad's novella about Captain MacWhirr's ship.

clue.text: Credos unusually recorded

indicators.note: unusually means in an unaccustomed way, so the word before it is put in an odd order

explanation.surface: Statements of belief were set down in an odd fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: To score is to tally or note down, as a game's points are written up.

clue.text: Acute co, dismantled for playwright

indicators.note: dismantled means taken apart, so the letters of the words before it are pulled to pieces and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A sharp company is broken up to make way for a dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Cocteau was a French dramatist, poet and filmmaker, author of Les Parents terribles.

clue.text: More so, but not necessarily wide

definitions.meaning: in cricket a wide is one kind of run conceded without the batsman hitting the ball; others are byes and no-balls

explanation.surface: Something additional that need not be broad.
explanation.definitionFit: An addition is something more, and in cricket a wide is one of several kinds of bonus run, not the only one.

clue.text: Dodie's family

parts.note: Dodie Smith's 1938 play Dear ... takes its title from a toast to the family, whose tentacles hold us

explanation.definitionFit: In Dodie Smith's play Dear Octopus, the family is toasted as a creature whose tentacles never let go.

clue.text: Shout about for a handyman in Australia

definitions.text: Shout about for a handyman in Australia

parts.words: Shout about for a handyman in Australia
parts.note: the word for shout, put before the word about, gives an odd-job worker on Australian sheep stations

explanation.walkthrough: To roust is to rout out or shout at; add 'about' and you get roustabout, an Australian station hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Rousting is raising a din to rout someone out, and with about it names an Australian station hand.

clue.text: Stories reiterated by Hawthorne

parts.note: Nathaniel Hawthorne's 1837 collection of short stories is titled ... Tales

explanation.definitionFit: Something reiterated has been said a second time, and Hawthorne's story collection is titled with this phrase.

clue.text: Yoga has a nasty way of concealing its positions

indicators.note: way of concealing says the words that follow contain the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: Yoga has an unpleasant habit of hiding the postures it uses.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'has a nasty'; asanas are the postures of hatha yoga.
explanation.definitionFit: In hatha yoga each held posture is an asana, the Sanskrit for seat.
